concepts.name: Flow rate
concepts.statement: Flow rate is the volume of fluid that passes a location through an area during a period of time, and it is the quantity almost every question about a moving fluid is asked in: how much blood a heart pumps, how much water a hose delivers, how much air a duct carries. Because it counts volume rather than distance, it tells you nothing on its own about how fast the fluid is moving or how wide the conduit is, only about the product of the two.

concepts.name: Converting flow rate units
concepts.statement: The SI unit of flow rate is the cubic meter per second, but almost nothing uses it: a heart pumps liters per minute, a fire hose delivers liters per second, and a capillary carries cubic centimeters per second. A liter is a thousandth of a cubic meter. Use whatever metric units are most convenient for the situation, and expect to convert between them in almost every problem.

concepts.name: Flow rate and velocity
concepts.statement: The flow rate is the cross-sectional area of the conduit times the average velocity of the fluid across it, $Q = A\bar{v}$. Flow rate and velocity are therefore related but different quantities: a wide, slow river can carry more water than a narrow, fast one.

concepts.name: Incompressible fluid
concepts.statement: A fluid is incompressible when a given amount of it always occupies the same volume, however hard it is pressed. Since liquids are essentially incompressible, the equation of continuity is valid for all of them; gases are compressible, and the equation must be applied to them with caution if they are subjected to compression or expansion. Every result of this chapter, Bernoulli’s equation and Poiseuille’s law included, is written for an incompressible fluid.

concepts.name: Equation of continuity
concepts.statement: Because the fluid is incompressible, the same amount of fluid must flow past any point of a tube in a given time, so the flow rate is the same at all points along it. Where the cross-sectional area decreases the velocity must necessarily increase, and where it increases the velocity drops. That is the purpose of a nozzle, and it is why water slows considerably when a river empties into a reservoir and picks up speed again when it leaves.

concepts.name: Continuity in branching flow
concepts.statement: In the cardiovascular system and in any other branching network, the flow does not stay in one tube. Continuity still holds, but for the sum of the flow rates in all the branches in any portion along the tube, so the number of branches enters the equation along with their areas and their speeds. The capillaries have an enormously greater total cross-section than the aorta, so the blood in them moves at about a millimeter per second. That is slow enough for the blood to exchange substances with the cells and still fast enough to avoid clotting.

concepts.name: Fluid dynamics
concepts.statement: Fluid dynamics is the physics of fluids in motion.

concepts.name: Liter
concepts.statement: A liter is a unit of volume equal to $10^{-3}\;\text{m}^3$, or 1000 cubic centimeters.

concepts.name: Pressure drop in a fast fluid
concepts.statement: Where a fluid speeds up, its pressure drops. A fluid flowing into a narrower channel gains kinetic energy, and that energy comes from the net work done by the higher pressure behind it pushing it into the channel.

concepts.name: Bernoulli’s equation
concepts.statement: Bernoulli’s equation states the relationship between pressure and velocity in a fluid quantitatively: for an incompressible, frictionless fluid the sum of the pressure, the term in the square of the speed and the term in the height is constant along the path a bit of fluid follows. Various quantities in the sum may change as the fluid moves, but the total does not, so a gain in speed or in height has to be paid for out of pressure.

forms.latex: P_1 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_1^2 + \rho gh_1 = P_2 + \frac{1}{2}\rho v_2^2 + \rho gh_2

concepts.name: Bernoulli’s equation as energy per volume
concepts.statement: Bernoulli’s equation is a form of the conservation of energy principle. The second and third terms are the kinetic and the gravitational potential energy with the mass replaced by the density, so each is an energy divided by a volume, and the pressure is an energy per unit volume too, since a newton per square meter multiplied by meter over meter is a joule per cubic meter. Bernoulli’s equation is, in fact, just a convenient statement of conservation of energy for an incompressible fluid in the absence of friction.

concepts.name: Bernoulli’s equation for a static fluid
concepts.statement: When the fluid is not moving, both speed terms vanish and Bernoulli’s equation says that pressure increases with depth: going down by a height adds the weight of that column of fluid to the pressure. In the simplest case the pressure at the top is zero, and you recover the familiar relationship for the pressure due to the weight of a fluid. So although Bernoulli’s equation describes fluid flow, it includes much of what the preceding chapter found for static fluids.

forms.condition: static fluid, with the lower point taken as the reference height

concepts.name: Bernoulli’s principle
concepts.statement: When a fluid moves but its depth is constant, the terms in the height subtract out and Bernoulli’s equation becomes a statement about pressure and speed alone. Situations of that kind are so important that the equation has a name of its own. It says what the opening of the section argued: if the speed at one point is greater, the pressure there must be less for the equality to hold.

concepts.name: Entrainment
concepts.statement: People have long put Bernoulli’s principle to work by using the reduced pressure in a high-velocity fluid to move things about: with a higher pressure on the outside, the fast stream forces other fluids into itself. Entrainment devices have been in use since ancient times as pumps to raise water small heights, and the same trick runs a Bunsen burner, an atomizer, a paint sprayer, an aspirator and the chimney of a water heater.

concepts.name: Lift on a wing
concepts.statement: The airplane wing is a beautiful example of Bernoulli’s principle in action. The wing tilts upward at a small angle and its upper surface is longer, so air flows faster over the top, the pressure there drops, and the difference is a net upward force. A sail has the characteristic shape of a wing too: the pressure on its front is lower than the pressure on its back, which gives a forward force and even lets a boat sail into the wind. Wings also gain lift by pushing air downward, and the deflected air pushes back on the wing by Newton’s third law.

concepts.name: Measuring fluid speed
concepts.statement: Two tubes small enough not to disturb the flow, joined by a manometer, measure the speed of a fluid. The tube facing the oncoming fluid creates a dead spot with zero velocity in front of it, while the fluid passing the other tube keeps its speed, so the pressure at the second opening is lower by the term in the square of the speed. The manometer fluid rises by a height proportional to that term, and the speed is therefore proportional to the square root of the height. The pitot tube built on this principle is the air speed indicator of an aircraft.

concepts.name: Torricelli’s theorem
concepts.statement: Fluid leaving a reservoir through an opening a height $h$ below its surface emerges at the speed it would have if it had fallen freely through that height, $v_2^2 = v_1^2 + 2gh$, whatever the size of the opening.

concepts.name: Applying Bernoulli’s equation
concepts.statement: Every earlier use of Bernoulli’s equation simplified it first, by holding the height constant or the pressure equal at both points. The general case keeps all three terms at both points. Find the speeds from the flow rate and the two cross-sections, measure the heights from whichever point you take as the reference, and solve for the remaining pressure. A fire hose that runs ten meters up a ladder to a narrow nozzle is exactly this case, and its pressure falls for both reasons at once.

concepts.name: Power in fluid flow
concepts.statement: Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is used or supplied. Every term of Bernoulli’s equation is an energy per unit volume, so multiplying the whole equation by the flow rate, which is a volume per unit time, gives a power. Each term then has a clear physical meaning: one is the power supplied to give the fluid its pressure, one the power supplied to give it its kinetic energy, and one the power that goes to gravitational potential energy.

concepts.name: Finding the power of a pump
concepts.statement: A pump that takes fluid in and sends it out through a hose of the same diameter at the same height changes neither the speed nor the height of the fluid. Its kinetic and gravitational potential energy stay the same, and only the pressure term remains. The power the pump supplies is then the pressure it adds multiplied by the flow rate. A pump that raises velocity and height as well, as the heart does, needs all three terms.

concepts.name: Laminar flow
concepts.statement: Laminar flow is characterized by the smooth flow of a fluid in layers that do not mix. The lines drawn in the figures of this chapter are streamlines, the paths followed by small volumes of fluid, and in laminar flow they are smooth and continuous. The precise definition of viscosity is based on laminar flow, and so is Poiseuille’s law, so the whole of this section assumes it.

concepts.name: Turbulent flow
concepts.statement: Turbulence is characterized by eddies and swirls that mix layers of fluid together, and its streamlines break up rather than running smoothly. It has two main causes: any obstruction or sharp corner imparts velocities perpendicular to the flow, and high speeds alone will do it, since the drag between adjacent layers and between the fluid and its surroundings forms swirls if the speed is great enough. Turbulent flow mixes the fluid, heats it more and resists more than laminar flow does.

concepts.name: Viscosity
concepts.statement: Viscosity is fluid friction, both within the fluid and between the fluid and its surroundings: juice pours freely and syrup sticks to the pitcher. It is measured by shearing a fluid between two plates, one held fixed and one moved at a steady speed, and finding the force that keeps the top plate moving. That force grows with the speed, with the area of the plate and with the viscosity, and falls as the plates are moved apart, so the viscosity is the force times the separation divided by the speed times the area. Viscosities vary from one fluid to another by several orders of magnitude, gases being far less viscous than liquids, and most of them depend on temperature.

concepts.name: Velocity profile in a tube
concepts.statement: If the flow in a tube has negligible resistance the speed is the same all across it. When a viscous fluid flows, the layer in contact with the wall does not move at all, and the speed increases steadily to its maximum at the center of the tube. The shape of a Bunsen burner flame is that velocity profile made visible, even though the viscosity of natural gas is small.

concepts.name: Resistance to flow
concepts.statement: The resistance to flow is defined by the relationship between flow rate and pressure difference: the flow rate is the pressure difference divided by the resistance, $Q = (P_2 - P_1)/R$, and it is in the direction from high to low pressure. The resistance includes everything except pressure that affects the flow rate.

concepts.name: Poiseuille’s law for resistance
concepts.statement: For laminar flow of an incompressible fluid through a horizontal tube of uniform radius, the resistance is eight times the viscosity times the length, divided by pi times the fourth power of the radius. Resistance directly proportional to viscosity and to length makes good intuitive sense, since both directly affect the amount of friction encountered. The fourth power of the radius is the surprise. J. L. Poiseuille derived the law in an attempt to understand the flow of blood.

forms.condition: laminar flow in a horizontal tube of uniform radius

concepts.name: Poiseuille’s law
concepts.statement: Putting the resistance into the relationship between flow rate and pressure difference gives one equation for laminar flow through a tube: the flow rate is the pressure difference times pi times the fourth power of the radius, divided by eight times the viscosity times the length. It is the working equation of the section, and of every medical application in the chapter.

forms.condition: laminar flow in a horizontal tube of uniform radius

concepts.name: Sensitivity of flow to radius
concepts.statement: The radius enters to the fourth power, so any change in it has a very large effect on the resistance. Doubling the radius decreases the resistance by a factor of sixteen, and reducing a vessel’s radius by only five percent cuts the flow to about eighty-one percent of its original value. That is why the body regulates blood flow mostly by dilating and constricting vessels rather than by working the heart harder, and why plaque in an artery is dangerous out of all proportion to its thickness. The body may compensate by raising the blood pressure, but that puts the heart and any weakened vessel at risk.

concepts.name: Pressure drop from resistance
concepts.statement: Rearranged, the relationship between flow rate, pressure difference and resistance says that flow through a resistance makes the pressure drop along it. That is why the water pressure in a house is lower on a hot summer day when the neighborhood draws heavily: the flow rate in the main is large, so the drop along it is large, and less pressure arrives. The relationship holds for turbulent as well as laminar flow. It also applies to a system whose radius varies, where the drop is greatest at the narrowest place.

concepts.name: Reynolds number for flow in a tube
concepts.statement: The Reynolds number for flow in a tube, $N_{\text{R}} = 2\rho vr/\eta$, is a dimensionless quantity that reveals whether the flow is likely to be laminar or turbulent.

forms.condition: flow in a tube of uniform diameter

concepts.name: Onset of turbulence
concepts.statement: For a Reynolds number below about 2000 the flow is laminar, and above about 3000 it is turbulent. Between 2000 and 3000 the flow is unstable: it can be laminar, but small obstructions and surface roughness can make it turbulent, and it may oscillate randomly between the two. Most of the blood flow in the body is quiet and laminar; the exception is the aorta, where the speed rises above a critical value and the flow becomes turbulent.

concepts.name: Turbulence in the circulatory system
concepts.statement: An occlusion or narrowing of an artery is likely to cause turbulence, both because of the irregularity of the blockage and because of the complexity of blood as a fluid. Turbulence in the circulatory system is noisy and can often be heard: the Korotkoff sounds heard through a stethoscope when a blood pressure cuff is released, the sounds of an aneurysm, and the heart murmurs made by damaged valves that do not close. Ultrasound detects the same turbulence in a way analogous to Doppler-shift radar detecting a storm.

concepts.name: Chaotic behavior
concepts.statement: A system is chaotic when its behavior is so sensitive to some factor that it is extremely difficult to predict. Flow with a Reynolds number between 2000 and 3000 is a good example: whether it is turbulent is difficult but not impossible to predict, and the difficulty lies in the extremely sensitive dependence on roughness and obstructions, where a tiny variation in one factor has an exaggerated effect on the flow. Phenomena as disparate as turbulence, the orbit of Pluto and the onset of irregular heartbeats are chaotic and can be analyzed with similar techniques.

concepts.name: Reynolds number for an object
concepts.statement: The Reynolds number for an object moving in a fluid, ${N'}_{\text{R}} = \rho vL/\eta$, where $L$ is a characteristic length of the object, indicates whether the flow around it is laminar or turbulent. A moving object in a still fluid is equivalent to a stationary object in a flowing stream.

concepts.name: Flow around an object
concepts.statement: Below about 1 the flow around an object can be laminar, particularly if the object has a smooth shape. Between 1 and about 10 the flow turns turbulent, the exact point depending on surface roughness, and a turbulent wake forms behind the object while some laminar flow remains over its surface. Between 10 and a million the flow may be either and may oscillate between the two, and above a million it is turbulent everywhere, even at the surface. Laminar flow occurs mostly when the objects are small, such as raindrops, pollen and blood cells in plasma, so most large objects, airplanes and sailboats among them, create significant turbulence as they move.

concepts.name: Viscous drag
concepts.statement: One of the consequences of viscosity is a resistance force called viscous drag, exerted on an object moving through a fluid. Unlike simple friction it depends on the object’s speed, and how it depends on it changes with the Reynolds number: for laminar flow the drag is proportional to the speed, while between about 10 and a million it is proportional to the speed squared, which is why even a small headwind costs a bicycle racer so much and why cyclists take turns leading the pack. For laminar flow around a sphere the drag is proportional to the viscosity, the size of the object and its speed, all of which makes sense, since the more viscous the fluid and the larger the object the more drag is to be expected; Stokes’ law gives the constant.

concepts.name: Sedimentation and the centrifuge
concepts.statement: Because the viscous drag grows with speed, an object falling through a fluid does not accelerate indefinitely. The drag increases, the acceleration falls, and at the terminal speed the object continues to fall at a constant speed. This is the case for particles of sand falling in the ocean, cells falling in a centrifuge and sky divers falling through the air, and the terminal speed is greatest for low-viscosity fluids and for objects that are dense and small, which is why a skydiver falls more slowly with outspread limbs than in a pike position. Knowing it is useful for estimating how quickly small particles settle, and a centrifuge speeds that settling by replacing gravitational acceleration with a much greater centripetal acceleration.

concepts.name: Diffusion
concepts.statement: Atoms and molecules are in constant motion at any temperature, and in fluids they move about randomly even where there is no macroscopic flow. That motion is a random walk, and diffusion is the movement of substances that it produces. It explains how an ice cube picks up the odors of a freezer, and fluids can even diffuse through solids. It is a slow process over macroscopic distances, because the densities of common materials are great enough that a molecule cannot travel far before a collision scatters it in any direction, including straight backward.

concepts.name: Diffusion distance
concepts.statement: The root-mean-square distance a molecule travels by diffusion is proportional to the square root of the time, $x_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{2Dt}$, not to the time itself, which is what makes diffusion so slow over any large distance.

concepts.name: Diffusion constant
concepts.statement: The diffusion constant is determined experimentally and gathers into one number most of the things that set the rate: the molecule, the medium, the temperature and the cohesive and adhesive forces. It gets progressively smaller for more massive molecules, because the average molecular speed at a given temperature is inversely proportional to molecular mass, and it is far smaller in water than in air, because a molecule in water makes many more collisions in its random walk. It increases with temperature, since the average kinetic energy of the molecules is proportional to absolute temperature.

concepts.name: Rate and direction of diffusion
concepts.statement: A drop of food coloring placed carefully in still water spreads until its concentration is the same everywhere, which is free diffusion, since no barrier inhibits it. Molecular motion is random in direction, so simple chance dictates that more molecules leave a region of high concentration than enter it, and the net rate of diffusion is proportional to the difference in concentration; if the concentrations were the same there would be no net movement at all. The net rate is higher at the start than after the process is partly complete, and it is proportional to the diffusion constant as well.

concepts.name: Semipermeable membranes
concepts.statement: A semipermeable membrane allows only certain small molecules to pass through it. Membranes in living things are generally of this kind, and they affect the rates at which substances diffuse across them.

concepts.name: Osmosis
concepts.statement: Osmosis is the transport of water through a semipermeable membrane from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration, and it is driven by the imbalance in water concentration. Water is more concentrated in the body than in Epsom salt, so soaking a swollen ankle in Epsom salt moves water out of the body into the lower-concentration region in the salt. Both osmosis and dialysis are used by the kidneys to cleanse the blood.

concepts.name: Dialysis
concepts.statement: Dialysis is the transport of any molecule other than water through a semipermeable membrane because of its concentration difference. It is the same process as osmosis with a different substance moving, and like osmosis it can create substantial pressures. The kidneys use both.

concepts.name: Osmotic pressure and back pressure
concepts.statement: Osmosis can create a substantial pressure. Water moving through a membrane raises the solution on the low-concentration side, and the movement continues until the pressure created by the extra height of fluid is large enough to stop further osmosis. That back pressure is called the relative osmotic pressure if neither solution is pure water and the osmotic pressure if one of them is, and it can be very large: pure water and sea water separated by a membrane that passes no salt come to equilibrium at 25.9 atmospheres, which would raise the salt water 268 meters above the pure water. Turgor, the pressure of a plant cell’s fluid against its wall, is the same effect holding a plant up. Where the back pressure is sufficient to reverse the normal direction, the process becomes reverse osmosis or reverse dialysis, which is how water is desalinated and how a membrane is used to filter.

concepts.name: Active transport
concepts.statement: Substances sometimes pass through a membrane in the direction opposite to the one expected. Cypress tree roots extract pure water from salt water although osmosis would move it the other way, and this is not reverse osmosis, because there is no back pressure to cause it. What is happening is active transport, a process in which a living membrane expends energy to move substances across it. Many living membranes do this, the kidneys among them, and it is estimated that at least a quarter of the body’s energy is expended on active transport at the cellular level.

concepts.name: Relative osmotic pressure
concepts.statement: Relative osmotic pressure is the back pressure that stops the osmotic process when neither solution is pure water.

concepts.name: Reverse osmosis
concepts.statement: Reverse osmosis is the process that occurs when back pressure is great enough to reverse the normal direction of osmosis, driving water out of the more concentrated solution. It is used to desalinate water by forcing it through a membrane that will not pass salt.

concepts.name: Reverse dialysis
concepts.statement: Reverse dialysis is the process that occurs when back pressure is great enough to reverse the normal direction of dialysis, and it can be used to filter out a substance that a membrane will not pass.
